tagline: Over 1,000 islands along the Dalmatian coast — the Adriatic's island highway.
summary: Croatia's Adriatic coast threads more than 1,000 islands along Dalmatia, from Split and the central islands of Brač and Hvar south to Korčula and the walled city of Dubrovnik. Island-hopping is the defining Croatian travel experience and a backbone of its tourism economy. Today it runs on car ferries and seasonal high-speed catamarans that fill through the summer. A clean, on-demand foiling tier is the premium layer between the timetabled catamaran and the chartered yacht.
why_marine_mobility: No single city brief tells the Croatian story, because it IS the Adriatic between Split, Hvar, Korčula and Dubrovnik. The summer islands move on catamarans that sell out on fixed schedules; the alternative is a chartered yacht or sailboat. Navier's Pioneer II foiling tier slots between them — an on-demand, dry, stabilised crossing that turns the island hop into a smooth glide — while the Quanta-LR hybrid range opens the long Adriatic trunk from Dalmatia toward Venice that no day-boat can serve.

demand_signals.label: Dalmatian island volume
demand_signals.note: Hvar, Brač, Korčula and the Split–Dubrovnik corridor draw heavy summer visitor traffic, the majority moving between islands by sea.

demand_signals.label: Yacht-charter hub
demand_signals.note: Dalmatia is one of the Mediterranean's fastest-growing yacht-charter and nautical-tourism markets; demand for fast, discreet premium transfers is structural.

demand_signals.label: Inhabited-island links
demand_signals.note: Dozens of inhabited Dalmatian islands depend on ferry connections for residents, goods and tourism — core infrastructure, not discretionary travel.

demand_signals.label: Catamaran schedule saturation
demand_signals.note: Summer high-speed catamaran routes run at capacity on fixed timetables — an on-demand premium tier relieves the bottleneck.

use_cases.body: Split to Hvar: the marquee central-Dalmatian crossing, today a busy catamaran on a fixed schedule — ideal for an on-demand, dry, premium foiling tier.
Korčula to Dubrovnik: a ~46-nautical-mile southern-Dalmatian link connecting the island chain to the walled city, comfortably inside Pioneer II range.
Split to Venice: a long-range Quanta-LR Adriatic trunk linking Dalmatia to the head of the Adriatic — a crossing reserved today for yachts.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The core Dalmatian crossings — Split–Hvar (25 nm), Brač–Hvar (~11 nm), Korčula–Dubrovnik (46 nm) — sit inside Pioneer II's 70-nautical-mile range at 30 knots, commercial-ready today.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The long Adriatic trunk from Split toward Venice (~211 nm) is Quanta-LR territory (~700 nm hybrid range, H2 2026+), opening a head-of-Adriatic corridor no battery day-boat can reach.

signature_routes.label: Split ↔ Hvar — the marquee Dalmatian crossing
Split ↔ Venice — the long-range Adriatic trunk

transit_planning: For a tourism authority or a premium operator: an on-demand, low-emission water tier that relieves the saturated summer catamaran schedule across Dalmatia and gives the island hop the comfort of a private craft at a shuttle's cadence. Start with the proven Split–Hvar–Korčula corridors on Pioneer II, then add the Venice trunk on Quanta-LR.
competitive_landscape: Island travel today splits between car ferries and high-speed catamarans (affordable, high-capacity, but timetabled and summer-saturated) and yacht / sailboat charter (flexible but costly). Navier's foiling tier is the missing on-demand middle: faster and drier than a catamaran, far more attainable than a charter, and cleaner than both.
regulatory_note: Croatian maritime transport is regulated by the Ministry of the Sea, Transport and Infrastructure and the harbour-master offices (lučke kapetanije), within EU maritime-safety frameworks; passenger operation requires vessel certification and route authorisation. The Split-Dalmatia and Dubrovnik-Neretva county authorities are natural first touchpoints.
seasonality: Peak season (Jun–Sep) drives the densest island traffic and the busiest catamaran schedules; the shoulder months (May, Oct) offer calmer seas and lighter loads. The Adriatic is generally sheltered, with the bura wind the main weather variable a stabilised craft is built to handle.

precedents.what: Four Seasons Lake Austin operates an N30 in live luxury-hospitality service — proof of the premium water-shuttle model Navier brings to the Dalmatian coast.
